A B S T R A C T

The rapid evolution of wireless communication technologies from 1G to 5G has enabled remarkable advances in
connectivity, yet emerging applications such as holographic telepresence, autonomous systems, wireless brain-
computer interfaces, and ubiquitous 3D coverage expose fundamental limitations in current networks.

While
numerous surveys have explored individual 6G enablers, few studies provide a unified and comprehensive
analysis that integrates the technological foundations, architectural transformations, and multidisciplinary
applications required to realize future 6G systems.

1. Introduction

The evolution of mobile communication networks has been one of
the most transformative technological journeys of the modern era [1].
Since the deployment of the first generation (1G) cellular networks
in the 1980s, each subsequent generation, 2G, 3G, 4G, and more
recently 5G, has introduced significant advancements in data rate,
latency, network capacity, and service capabilities. These generational
shifts have not only enhanced user experience but also catalyzed the
proliferation of mobile-based services and digital ecosystems. Driven
by rapid advancements in hardware, spectrum utilization, and protocol
design, the mobile network landscape has continuously evolved to
meet the ever-growing demand for connectivity and mobility in both
personal and industrial domains [2].

Building on this foundation, the survey offers a holistic and structured review of essential 6G enabling technologies, including terahertz
communication, ultra-massive MIMO, intelligent reflective surfaces,
AI-native networking, edge intelligence, Digital Twin Networks, and
generative artificial intelligence, emphasizing their roles, advantages,
and open research challenges.

In addition, the paper delivers a detailed analysis of next-generation network architectures by presenting
an integrated perspective of space-air-ground-sea systems, highlighting architectural design principles, major components, interoperability
constraints, and system-level considerations.

The manuscript further
examines a broad set of emerging 6G application domains such as
extended reality, autonomous systems, intelligent healthcare, the Internet of Everything, and holographic communication.

To illustrate the
practical relevance of these technologies, a realistic end-to-end scenario
of 6G-enabled remote holographic surgery is presented, demonstrating
how multiple 6G enablers converge to support mission-critical operations.

granting users access to the vast realm of the internet. This transformation enabled an array of advanced services previously unsupported
by the 1G and 2G networks, including web browsing, TV streaming,

these requirements by not only increasing network performance but
also enabling new paradigms of connectivity that integrate advanced
technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML),
and quantum communication into the core of the network [21].

advanced capabilities. 3GPP Release 18, published in 2024, represent

AI is set to become one of the foundations of 6G networks, enabling intelligent decision-making and optimization across the network.
From resource allocation to interference management, AI will empower
6G systems with self-learning and adaptive capabilities. Key applications include autonomous network configuration, anomaly detection,
and predictive maintenance. AI facilitates enhanced user experience
through personalized services and dynamic quality-of-service (QoS)
adjustments. AI also enables closed-loop optimization to wireless 6G
networks. In this technique, the user acts in accordance with device
feedback. By maintaining end-to-end collective optimization at the
system layer, AI can further be implemented to optimize wireless
communication systems. This intelligent layer offers numerous possibilities, such as self-optimization, self-learning, and data collection. These
examples are only a small part of the widespread applications of AI
technologies and the innovations they will bring to the 6G network
structure [32].

4.2. Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI)

Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is poised to play a critical
role in 6G, enabling the creation, prediction, and synthesis of complex
network information using advanced generative models such as GANs,
VAEs, diffusion models, and large language models (LLMs). Unlike traditional AI, which primarily performs classification or regression tasks,
GenAI can generate realistic channel models, mobility patterns, network traffic predictions, synthetic training datasets, and even optimized
communication waveforms [34].

The Terahertz (THz) band, presented in Fig. 5, spanning 0.1-10
THz, represents the last untapped region in the radio frequency spectrum, offering ultra-high bandwidth and data rates up to 1 Tbps. It
bridges the gap between millimeter-wave (mmWave) and infrared (IR)
frequencies, combining broader transmission bandwidth than mmWave
with better propagation characteristics than IR. THz communication
is essential for 6G, enabling applications such as holographic telepresence, and ultra-HD streaming [37].

With its ability to support ultra-dense networks and massive capacity, THz communication is poised to meet 6G's demands for unprecedented data rates and low latency. Advantages include higher spectral
efficiency, integration of thousands of small antenna elements into
base stations, and enhanced security through high directional beams.
However, challenges like system complexity, power consumption, and
THz component design must be addressed. Leveraging advancements
like ultra-massive MIMO and Intelligent Reflective Surfaces, THz communication is a promising enabler for 6G networks [38].

The Terahertz (THz) band, presented in Fig. 5, spanning 0.1-10
THz, represents the last untapped region in the radio frequency spectrum, offering ultra-high bandwidth and data rates up to 1 Tbps. It
bridges the gap between millimeter-wave (mmWave) and infrared (IR)
frequencies, combining broader transmission bandwidth than mmWave
with better propagation characteristics than IR. THz communication
is essential for 6G, enabling applications such as holographic telepresence, and ultra-HD streaming [37].

efficiency, integration of thousands of small antenna elements into
base stations, and enhanced security through high directional beams.
However, challenges like system complexity, power consumption, and
THz component design must be addressed. Leveraging advancements
like ultra-massive MIMO and Intelligent Reflective Surfaces, THz communication is a promising enabler for 6G networks [38].

Visual Light Communication (VLC) uses visible light as a wireless
communication medium, offering high data rates, immunity to electromagnetic interference, and secure, interference-free communication.
It is especially suitable for indoor environments like hospitals and
factories, and it complements traditional systems [39].

VLC operates similarly to fiber optics, delivering fiber-like transmission rates and bandwidth through light. With terahertz-level bandwidth, high-frequency reuse, and unlicensed spectrum, VLC supports
gigabit-level transmission. However, current systems face challenges
like narrow LED bandwidths and the need for efficient ultra massive
MIMO designs.

Despite these hurdles, advancements in VLC are expected to enable
terabit-level data rates for 6G by 2030, utilizing thousands of LED
active sources for short-range, high-capacity communication [40].

Intelligent Reflective Surfaces (IRS) are reconfigurable metasurfaces
designed to enhance wireless communication by passively reflecting
electromagnetic waves towards desired directions, as illustrated in
Fig. 7. Composed of numerous low-cost reflective elements, IRS can

dynamically control the phase of incident signals without requiring
active transmission or significant power consumption [49].

IRS significantly improves signal propagation in challenging scenarios such as non-line-of-sight (NLOS) and deep-fade environments
by increasing the signal to interference and noise ratio (SINR). These
surfaces can be strategically deployed on buildings, vehicles, and other
structures to enhance coverage and reliability without modifying existing infrastructure. Applications include beam steering, beamforming,
and multi-user communication, with performance further enhanced
through integration with machine learning techniques such as deep
learning and neural networks.

By complementing massive MIMO, a key 5G technology, IRS contributes to improved spectral efficiency and higher data rates, positioning it as an important component in future 6G networks [46].

5.1.1. Space network: LEO satellite systems
High-Throughput Satellite (HTS) systems now offer broadband Internet services with cost and bandwidth performance comparable to
terrestrial networks. However, most communication satellites operate in geostationary orbit (GEO) at 35,786 km altitude, resulting in
high latency and integration challenges with terrestrial mobile networks. To overcome these limitations, Non-Geostationary Orbit (NGSO)
satellite systems - such as those in Low Earth Orbit (LEO) and
Medium Earth Orbit (MEO) - have been proposed to provide global,
low-latency, high-throughput Internet connectivity [60]. Major NGSO
initiatives include: Starlink, with over 11,000 planned satellites by
2027 [8]; OneWeb, targeting a 720-satellite LEO constellation; and
China's Hongyan project, expected to deploy 320 satellites by 2025.

Though large-scale deployment and integration of NGSO systems
with terrestrial networks are still in progress, theoretical and simulation
results demonstrate their potential. Notably, LEO satellite networks
with laser and RF co-routing can outperform terrestrial fiber links in
latency over distances greater than 3000 km.

To enable global connectivity, the Space-Terrestrial Integrated Network (STIN) architecture has been introduced, comprising space-based
backbone networks (SBN), terrestrial networks (TN), and space-based
access networks (SAN) [61]. In this model, GEO satellites (SBN) ensure
wide-area coverage with inter-satellite links (ISLs), while LEO and MEO
satellites (SAN) facilitate integration with HTS and terrestrial networks
for ubiquitous access.

Emerging technologies play a key role in enhancing STIN functionality. Software-Defined Networking (SDN) and Information-Centric
Networking (ICN) offer adaptive control, efficient configuration, and
reduced latency. Additionally, Multipath TCP (MPTCP) ensures high
throughput and robust mobility management through seamless handover capabilities, as validated in recent evaluations.

To ensure stable global connectivity, future LEO networks will be
deeply integrated with terrestrial cores using SDN/NFV paradigms.
AI-driven route prediction will mitigate Doppler effects and optimize
inter-satellite link utilization, while Digital Twin models will help
operators evaluate constellation performance, simulated failures, and
congestion management strategies.

content:
The deployment of undersea communication systems presents several significant challenges due to the highly unpredictable and dynamic
nature of the underwater environment. Establishing stable network
connectivity is inherently difficult, as water conditions can change
rapidly with variations in temperature, salinity, turbidity, and ocean
currents, all of which affect signal propagation and system performance. Moreover, underwater channels suffer from severe signal attenuation, particularly for radio frequency and optical communication,
while acoustic signals, although capable of long-range transmission,
experience low data rates and high latency. The extreme physical conditions of deep-sea environments, including high pressure, corrosion,
and biofouling, further increase the risk of equipment degradation or
failure. These factors make network setup, maintenance, and longterm operation considerably more complex than in terrestrial or aerial
communication scenarios, highlighting the need for robust designs,
adaptive communication techniques, and resilient hardware capable of
withstanding harsh underwater conditions.

6G mobile technology introduces significant advancements, including high bandwidth, ultra-reliable communication, increased data rates,
low latency, and an ideal environment for AI integration. These enhancements open up new application areas, ranging from military uses
to meeting personal needs, particularly in scenarios requiring remote
services, as highlighted during the pandemic. The demand for reliable
communication with high data rates has become increasingly critical.

The advancement of Collaborative Robotics and Autonomous Systems (CRAS) is a major driver in the development of 6G networks. CRAS
includes emerging technologies such as autonomous vehicles, drone
swarms, flying delivery systems, and robotic platforms, all of which
impose stringent requirements on network performance beyond those
addressed by traditional IoT services in 5G (example in Fig. 13) [63].

The Internet of Everything (IoE) extends the concept of the Internet
of Things (IoT) by integrating people, data, processes, and devices into
a unified intelligent network. Through interconnected sensing devices,
IoE facilitates real-time identification, monitoring, and decision-making
across diverse environments, generating actionable insights for smarter
systems and services. These sensors are capable of capturing a broad
array of physical and biological parameters, enabling applications in
healthcare, smart cities, and industrial automation [66].

As IoE scales to billions of interconnected elements, it imposes
stringent requirements on network performance, including scalability,
reliability, and latency. Sixth-generation (6G) networks are positioned
as a key enabler for IoE, offering ultra-reliable low-latency communication (URLLC) and enhanced mobile broadband (eMBB) to support
real-time, high-throughput, and energy-efficient connectivity. Consequently, 6G will be essential in unlocking the full potential of IoE in
future hyper-connected environments.

have been extensively utilized in defense and military operations for
applications such as remotely operated aircraft and autonomous drones.
Over the years, the versatility of UAVs has extended their use into
civilian domains, including disaster relief, agricultural plantation protection, traffic monitoring, and environmental sensing. These applications have highlighted the potential of UAVs as indispensable tools in
addressing critical societal and environmental challenges [67].

With the emergence of 6G and the Internet of Everything (IoE),
UAVs are anticipated to evolve further into a UAV-to-Everything (U2X)
network. This paradigm shift will enable UAVs to connect seamlessly
with other devices and systems, expanding their utility beyond traditional communication. By leveraging advanced 6G capabilities such
as ultra-low latency, high data rates, and massive connectivity, UAVs
will optimize sensing applications and enhance their communication

7.1.1. High-frequency communication and propagation loss
6G networks are projected to operate in the sub-terahertz (sub-THz)
and terahertz (THz) frequency bands (100 GHz-10 THz) to support
data rates exceeding 1 Tbps. However, electromagnetic waves in this
frequency spectrum are highly susceptible to propagation losses due
to atmospheric absorption (e.g., water vapor, oxygen molecules) and
molecular scattering. These losses significantly limit the transmission
range and coverage area. Additionally, such high-frequency signals
experience increased vulnerability to multipath fading, non-line-ofsight (NLOS) conditions, and physical obstructions, necessitating the
development of advanced beamforming, intelligent reflecting surfaces
(IRS), and channel equalization techniques.

To meet the demands of ultra-dense connectivity and spatial multiplexing, 6G will employ ultra-massive multiple-input multiple-output
(UM-MIMO) systems, potentially involving thousands of antenna elements. While this allows for high spectral efficiency and energyefficient communication, it also introduces considerable challenges in

and hardware calibration. The increased dimensionality leads to high
computational complexity and makes real-time signal processing and
resource allocation significantly more difficult. Efficient and scalable
algorithms, possibly leveraging machine learning, are necessary for
practical implementation..

6G envisions a fully integrated communication framework that
combines terrestrial networks with non-terrestrial components, including low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites, high-altitude platforms (HAPs),

seamless interoperability and reliable service delivery.

7.1.5. Dynamic channel conditions
Due to high user mobility, frequent changes in network topology, and sensitivity to environmental conditions (e.g., rain, fog, or
urban clutter), 6G wireless channels are expected to be highly nonstationary and dynamic. These variations result in time-varying ISI,
Doppler effects, and unpredictable interference patterns. Consequently,
traditional static channel models are inadequate, necessitating the
adoption of real-time channel modeling, environment-aware communication protocols, and AI-based predictive algorithms to ensure robust
performance.

demand for higher speeds, lower latency, and ubiquitous connectivity,
6G aims to redefine how we interact with digital technologies and
the physical world. This paper has surveyed the fundamental enabling
technologies, including artificial intelligence, terahertz communication,
intelligent reflective surfaces, edge computing, and satellite integration,
that are expected to power 6G systems. In doing so, it has highlighted
how these innovations will address the growing needs of emerging
applications such as extended reality, autonomous systems, holographic
telepresence, and wireless brain-computer interfaces.

Beyond the technological vision, the paper has also addressed the
significant theoretical and practical challenges that must be overcome,
including spectrum limitations, energy efficiency, complex channel
dynamics, and the need for intelligent, adaptive network architectures. These obstacles demand a multi-disciplinary approach, combining advancements in communication engineering, artificial intelligence,
quantum computing, signal processing, and sustainable network design.

As we look towards the 2030 horizon, 6G is poised to become more
than just a faster network, it will be the foundation of a truly intelligent,
interconnected, and immersive digital ecosystem. Continued research
and collaboration across academia, industry, and government will be
essential in shaping the future of 6G and unlocking its transformative
potential for society.

Looking ahead, several research directions are expected to play
a decisive role in shaping the evolution of 6G networks. A primary
avenue involves the development of AI-native architectures and protocols capable of embedding intelligence, self-adaptation, and predictive
decision-making directly into the core of the communication system.

Addressing the limitations of high-frequency propagation will also
require continued exploration of hybrid THz-optical communication
models to support reliable, scalable terabit-class data transmission.

Moreover, realizing seamless global coverage will depend on advanced
cross-layer optimization strategies for space-air-ground-sea integrated
networks, enabling intelligent spectrum management, efficient resource
allocation, and robust mobility support across heterogeneous platforms.

Energy efficiency remains a critical priority, motivating further innovation in ultra-massive MIMO, RIS-assisted communication, and lowpower hardware design to ensure sustainable large-scale deployments.

Security and privacy concerns will likewise demand attention, particularly through the development of quantum-resistant cryptographic
schemes, blockchain-enabled trust mechanisms, and privacy-preserving
learning frameworks.

Finally, real-world prototypes and testbeds, especially for holographic communication, remote surgery, and brain-
computer interfaces, will be essential to validate theoretical concepts
and accelerate the practical realization of 6G technologies.
